Both OpenZeppelin and Geth are foundational contributions to the Ethereum ecosystem, though they operate at different layers. OpenZeppelin has significantly improved application security by standardizing battle-tested smart contract implementations and best practices, enabling broad ecosystem adoption. Geth, as the longest-running and most widely adopted Ethereum client, has played a critical role in defining protocol implementation standards, interoperability, operational reliability, and network stability. While both projects have had substantial ecosystem impact, Geth's role as a credibly neutral protocol-layer infrastructure may provide greater long-term strategic significance.

Foundry has evolved into a comprehensive Ethereum development platform, encompassing testing, deployment, local execution, debugging, CI, and infrastructure tooling. Its Rust-based ecosystem has also influenced a new generation of developer tools and workflows. In contrast, hardhat-deploy is a valuable project that promotes robust deployment practices within the Hardhat ecosystem, but its scope remains primarily focused on deployment workflows. Geth, by contrast, directly safeguards protocol correctness, asset security, network reliability, and operational continuity. As Ethereum’s most influential execution client and long-standing reference implementation, it has shaped protocol standards, interoperability, testing practices, and client reliability. Without secure and stable execution clients, applications would have little foundation to build upon.

Specs define the protocol itself, establishing the foundations of Proof-of-Stake, consensus, finality, and network correctness. In contrast, MEV-Boost introduced a practical architecture that mitigated some of the adverse effects of transaction ordering after Ethereum's transition to PoS, reducing certain forms of harmful MEV extraction while enabling a competitive builder ecosystem. I would suggest in general that account abstraction, ERC-4337 in particular, has been more valuable than smart contract verification. In its domain, the eth-infinitism implementation appears to be regularly referenced in other account abstraction material, and has significantly stronger github metrics (e.g. stars) than similar projects. In its domain, I seem to find that Act is well respected but may not see as much use as other related projects. Let's give account-abstraction a 2x factor for domain and a 3x factor for intra-domain impact.

Fe shows a lot of promise but has yet to see significant adoption. The Ethereum execution-apis are a critical part of Ethereum client specification. For the purpose of these comparisons, I imagine the value of the execution-apis repo and spec should be separated from the value of the execution clients themselves and much of the discussion and process that goes into determining the specs. Still, with this GitHub repo as a shared trustworthy location for spec reference, its value still greatly outweighs that of Fe's contributions to date. Though it's hard to put a number on it, I think this order of magnitude is about correct.

I tend to think that a large portion of the weight in determining the credit multiplier in these client-client comparisons comes down to simply having a complete, robust, reputable, and sufficiently efficient implementation. Any team that meets that baseline shouldn't be rated too far off from any other baseline-meeting team. Both of these clients satisfy that. However, geth in particular stands out not just as a reputable client but as one with a long history, and for better or worse has been seen as something closer to a reference implementation for the others. It is by far the most frequently forked EL client for teams building other EL chains, and that comes with additional reputational value and responsibility for the team. I would say that adds up to twice the impact of your average client.

This is a very apples-and-oranges comparison, and neither project is conducive to clear metrics of adoption. While helm charts are undeniably convenient to have, and a well-maintained repo with charts for common tools can reduce a lot of friction, ultimately I don't know if the impact on the "success of Ethereum" adds up to a lot. Not every project needs to be groundbreaking. The eth-infinitism account-abstraction implementation is more foundational to AA efforts (which as a whole are valuable), indicated by its stars, dependent repos, and wider reputation. 8x feels about right--I'd exchange this account-abstraction repo for ~8 repos which each support devops to the extent that these helm charts do.

Sourcify, as a smart contract code verification tool, is in an important space for Ethereum's values. It stands out in its space for being open-source (though it's not the only one) and offering a few unique features, has good GitHub metrics and reputation elsewhere on the web. Checkpoint sync is truly important for node operators today, especially home stakers dealing with high complexity and limited bandwidth, though. Checkpointz is not the only way to perform a checkpoint sync or offer your nodes as a sync endpoint, and so should not take on the value of the feature in general, but notably *every* mainnet endpoint on the eth-clients list ( https://eth-clients.github.io/checkpoint-sync-endpoints/ ) appears to run Checkpointz. A very useful tool, though the success of Ethereum does not depend on it as much it does on having reputable contract code verification software. Inter-domain I'd place verification at 4x the value of checkpoint sync tooling. Intra-domain sourcify is valuable but there are viable alternatives, while checkpointz really defines its category, which I'd say roughly balances out 1:1 for a total of 4x.
